title.narrative: Public Health Emergency Preparedness - Continuation and Upscaling of Health Assistance to the Syrian Population

description.narrative: ltpgtltbrgtSyria remains at high risk of Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) and cholera due to a combination of ongoing political instability, population displacement, and deteriorating public health infrastructure. The situation is further exacerbated by cross-border movement with Iraq, an ongoing economic crisis, disrupted water and sanitation services, and prolonged drought conditions leading to water scarcity. A resurgence of cholera was reported in 2024, following an outbreak initially declared in September 2022. ltigtltbgtThe outbreak has been attributed to damage to water and sanitation infrastructure, limited access to healthcare, and contaminated water sources in some governorates and locations. Between August and December 2024, Syria reported 1,444 suspected cholera cases with 7 deaths. The most affected governorates were Lattakia (382 cases, 26.5%), Hassaka (294 cases, 20.4%), Aleppo (280 cases, 19.4%), Deir-ez-Zor (215 cases, 14.9%) and Rural Damascus (80 cases, 5.5%). Additionally, Al-Hol camp reported 254 suspected cases and one associated death, highlighting the vulnerability of displaced populations.lt/bgtlt/igtltbrgtWith the proposed allocation WHO will work to expand access to and provision of quality, equitable, and integrated life-saving health services across all levels of care, including medical supply chain and equipment. Efforts and investments will also continue to enhance the health sector’s capacity to prepare for, detect, and deliver a timely response to disease outbreaks. WHO will also, given the changed circumstances in Syria, seek to strengthen and mainstream early recovery interventions to contribute to Syria’s health system resilience, including efforts focused on accountability to affected populations and localization approach. The project will focus on Epidemiology and Disease Surveillance, provision of Laboratory diagnostics for confirmation of cases of priority diseases, Risk communication and community engagement, and Logistics, Equipment, and Supplies for enhanced preparedness and response for outbreaks. ltigtltbgtWHO will also further strengthen the safety of consumed water as preventive approach to curb water transmitted diseases.nbsplt/bgtlt/igtltbrgtOver a 6-month period in Aleppo, Lattakia, Hassakeh, and Damascus, WHO will assist the Ministry of Health in enhancing public health surveillance for Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD). The project will strengthen rapid response teams and public health labs for cholera confirmation when AWD cases arise. WHO will procure supplies for cholera diagnosis, hygiene promotion, and AWD/cholera response, as well as sustain WASH activities to mitigate waterborne disease risks through water quality monitoring in high-risk areas. They will collaborate with the community and MoH to gather useful information for interventions and conduct awareness-raising activities. Surveillance will be part of the EWARS system, with operational support for Rapid Response Teams to address public health alerts promptly. The WASH component will be executed by WHO field staff using water quality monitoring tools.ltbrgt ltbrgt lt/pgt
